Quadrilateral, kite

questions.question_text: Is every rectangle also a parallelogram?

options.text: Yes — a rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, which is all a parallelogram requires.
Yes — every parallelogram has four right angles, just as a rectangle does.
options.why: Reaches the right verdict from a false property: a parallelogram need not have any right angles.

options.text: No — a shape that is a rectangle cannot also be given another name.
options.why: Treats the special names as competing labels instead of a hierarchy of nested types.

options.text: No — a parallelogram must have sloping sides, and a rectangle has none.
options.why: Judges from a typical picture of a parallelogram rather than from its defining property.

questions.solution_text:
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
The four right angles of a rectangle force both pairs of opposite sides to be parallel.
Yes — a rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, which is all a parallelogram requires.

questions.question_text: Which one of these statements is always true?

options.why: Reverses the inclusion; the sides of a parallelogram need not all be equal.
Reverses the inclusion; the two pairs of equal sides of a kite can be different lengths.
Reverses the inclusion; the adjacent sides of a rectangle need not be equal.

questions.solution_text:
A parallelogram needs both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
The four equal sides of a rhombus make both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so the rhombus always meets that requirement.
Every rhombus is a parallelogram.

questions.question_text: Which reason explains why every square is also a kite?

options.text: A square has four equal sides, so it has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
A square has four right angles, and a kite has two right angles.
options.why: Invents a right-angle requirement for the kite, which has none in its definition.

options.text: A square has two pairs of parallel sides, and so does a kite.
options.why: Gives the kite parallel sides, which are not part of the definition of a kite.

options.text: A square is a rectangle, and every rectangle is a kite.
options.why: Chains through the rectangle, but a rectangle is a kite only when all four of its sides are equal.

questions.solution_text:
A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
The four equal sides of a square include the two sides meeting at one vertex and the two meeting at the opposite vertex.
A square has four equal sides, so it has two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

questions.question_text: Why is a rhombus not always a square?

options.text: Its four angles need not be right angles.
Its four sides need not be equal.
options.why: Confuses the rhombus with the parallelogram; every rhombus has four equal sides.

options.text: Its opposite sides need not be parallel.
options.why: Denies a property every rhombus has, since a rhombus is always a parallelogram.

options.text: Its equal sides are adjacent rather than opposite.
options.why: Describes the kite property a rhombus also has, which does not stop it being a square.

questions.solution_text:
A square needs four equal sides and four right angles.
A rhombus is guaranteed only the four equal sides.
Its four angles need not be right angles.

questions.question_text: A quadrilateral is a rectangle, and it is also a kite. What is the most specific name for this shape?

options.why: Combines the two to get four equal sides but drops the right angles the rectangle guarantees.
Keeps the more familiar of the two names instead of combining both sets of properties.
Names the shape from the kite condition alone and ignores the four right angles of the rectangle.

questions.solution_text:
A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides, and a rectangle has its opposite sides equal.
Together these force all four sides to be equal.
Four equal sides with the four right angles of the rectangle give a square.
Square
